newsitem.title: JAPAN: TOKYO STOCKS SEEN LOSING GROUND ON YEN, WALL ST.
newsitem.headline: TOKYO STOCKS SEEN LOSING GROUND ON YEN, WALL ST.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to lose ground on Monday, as the yen's advance against the dollar and a sell-off in Wall Street stocks on Friday are expected to hurt Japan's leading export-oriented issues, brokers said.
Sentiment toward shares oriented to the domestic economy will also bearish due to recent economic indicators showing few signs of a vigorous economic recovery, they added.
On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average gained 128.61 points or 0.66 percent to close at 19,604.46. September Nikkei futures finished 310 points higher at 19,680.
"The higher yen and New York's tumble are likely to hit shares of electronics makers," said Kenji Karikomi, deputy general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.
"But the Nikkei 225 would be supported around 19,300, as there are several technical support lines standing around that level," he said.
A market analyst at a foreign securities house said that the benchmark Nikkei index may test 19,233, a low hit last week.
If the index breaches that point, the next support level would be the psychologically important 19,000, brokers said.
On Friday in New York, the Dow industrials slid 156.78 points to end at 8,031.22. It was the ninth-largest point decline in a single session in the blue-chip average's history.
The dollar was quoted around 115.45 yen at Tokyo midday on Monday, against 118.42/52 yen in late Tokyo trade on Friday. In New York, the U.S. currency closed at 114.75/85 on Friday.
By midday, Yamaichi Securities' shares had gained 23 yen or 10.04 percent to 252 yen, making the issue the second-sharpest gainer on the first section.
Its volume of 3.096 million shares made it the fourth-most heavily traded on the first section.
Brokers said the rebound in Yamaichi's shares in the morning was mainly prompted by short-term buying back on the news of management changes.

"But I expect the shares not to fall sharply from this level, as there are hopes that Yamaichi will possibly tie up with a foreign brokerage," said a trader at a Japanese second-tier securities house.

In a statement released after the midday close, Yamaichi said some of the resignations were also motivated by the brokerage's efforts to restructure its management in response to Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
Among exporters, leading Japanese technology shares dropped in active trading, hit by the higher yen against the dollar and U.S. stocks' tumble, traders said.

By midday, shares of leading computer maker Fujitsu Ltd were down 60 yen at 1,590. Hitachi Ltd, a leading electronic machinery maker, was down 40 yen at 1,280, while NEC Corp, another computer maker, was down 30 yen at 1,550.
By sector, deliners were led by precision instruments, communications, and fisheries. There were no major gainers.
